commas-1.title: Commas in a list
commas-1.rule: Use commas to separate three or more things in a list. Most books and schools put a comma before the last and or or (the Oxford comma). Newspapers often leave it out. Either way is right here, but use it in your schoolwork.
commas-1.example: We saw ducks, geese, and swans.

commas-2.title: Commas with clauses
commas-2.rule: When a sentence starts with a part like When, If, After or Because, put a comma after that part. Put a comma before and, but or so when it joins two complete sentences.
commas-2.example: When the bell rang, we lined up, and Ms. Cruz smiled.

commas-3.title: Commas and colons
commas-3.rule: Put a comma after yes, no or well at the start. Use commas around the name of the person you're talking to. Use a colon before a list when the words before it could be a sentence.
commas-3.example: Yes, Sam, bring three things: a coat, boots, and a snack.

dialogue-1.title: Quotation marks
dialogue-1.rule: Put quotation marks around the exact words someone says. When the speaker comes first, put a comma after said.

dialogue-2.title: Speaker at the end
dialogue-2.rule: When the speaker comes after the words, end the spoken words with a comma inside the quotation marks. A question mark or exclamation point stays.
dialogue-2.example: "I'm hungry," said Max. "Are you ready?" asked Mom.

dialogue-3.title: Split quotations
dialogue-3.rule: When the speaker splits one spoken sentence, use commas on both sides of the speaker and keep going in lowercase. If the speaker comes between two sentences, use a period and a capital letter.
dialogue-3.example: "If it rains," said Ava, "we'll stay in." "It's over," said Kai. "Let's go."

apostrophes-1.title: Owners and contractions
apostrophes-1.rule: Add 's to show that something belongs to one person or thing. An apostrophe also shows where letters are left out: do not becomes don't.
apostrophes-1.example: Maya's bike isn't in the garage.

apostrophes-2.title: More than one owner
apostrophes-2.rule: If a plural word already ends in s, add only an apostrophe. If it doesn't end in s, add 's.
apostrophes-2.example: The girls' team carried the children's books.

apostrophes-3.title: Sound-alike words
apostrophes-3.rule: Words that show ownership never use an apostrophe: its, their, your, whose. The apostrophe words are short for two words: it's = it is, they're = they are, you're = you are, who's = who is.
apostrophes-3.example: It's time for the dog to eat its dinner.

verbs-1.title: Past tense verbs
verbs-1.rule: Most verbs add -ed to tell about the past: walk becomes walked. Some verbs change in their own way: run becomes ran, bring becomes brought, catch becomes caught.
verbs-1.example: Yesterday we ran to the park and caught a frog.

verbs-2.title: Verbs that keep going
verbs-2.rule: Use was or were with an -ing verb for something that kept going in the past. Use am, is or are for right now, and will be for the future.
verbs-2.example: I was eating when the phone rang. Now I am drawing. Tomorrow I will be swimming.

verbs-3.title: Keep the tense steady
verbs-3.rule: When something happens in the past, keep every verb in the past. When it happens now, keep them in the present. Change the tense only when the time really changes.
verbs-3.example: We hiked to the lake, and then we swam until dinner.

agreement-1.title: Subjects and verbs match
agreement-1.rule: One person or thing gets a verb with -s: the dog barks. More than one gets a verb without -s: the dogs bark. I and you use the verb without -s.
agreement-1.example: My brother plays soccer. My sisters play softball.

agreement-2.title: Match in longer sentences
agreement-2.rule: In a sentence with two parts, check each subject with its own verb. Two subjects joined by and are more than one.
agreement-2.example: Kim and Jo ride bikes, but Sam walks.

agreement-3.title: Tricky subjects
agreement-3.rule: Find the real subject. Words like of the crayons can sit between the subject and the verb, but they aren't the subject. Each, everyone and nobody mean one.
agreement-3.example: The box of crayons is on the shelf. Everyone is ready.

pronouns-1.title: Reflexive pronouns
pronouns-1.rule: Use myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves or themselves when the one doing the action also gets the action. Hisself and theirselves aren't used in standard English.
pronouns-1.example: Ben made himself a sandwich, and we helped ourselves to grapes.

pronouns-2.title: Pronouns that match
pronouns-2.rule: A pronoun has to match the word it stands for. For one: he, she, it, his, her, its. For more than one: they, them, their.
pronouns-2.example: The girls packed their bags. Leo zipped his own coat.

pronouns-3.title: Who, which, that, where, when
pronouns-3.rule: Use who for people, which or that for things, whose to show who owns something, where for places and when for times.
pronouns-3.example: The girl who won lives in the town where I was born.

fragments-1.title: Complete sentences
fragments-1.rule: A complete sentence has five parts: a subject, a verb, a complete thought, a capital letter and an end mark. A fragment is missing something, so it doesn't make sense alone.
fragments-1.example: Fragment: Ran to the park. Complete: My dog ran to the park.

fragments-2.title: Fixing fragments
fragments-2.rule: A part that starts with because, when, after or if can't stand alone. Fix it by joining it to a complete sentence.
fragments-2.example: Because it was raining. becomes We stayed inside because it was raining.

fragments-3.title: Run-ons
fragments-3.rule: A run-on jams two complete sentences together. Fix it with a period, or with a comma and a joining word like and, but or so. A comma alone isn't enough.
fragments-3.example: The game ended late we were tired. becomes The game ended late, so we were tired.

compound-1.title: Joining with and, but, so
compound-1.rule: Join two complete sentences with and, but or so. And adds more, but shows a difference, and so tells what happened because of it. Put a comma before the joining word.
compound-1.example: It was hot, so we went swimming.

compound-2.title: Pick the best joining word
compound-2.rule: Choose the joining word that fits the meaning: and adds, but or yet shows a difference, or gives a choice, and so tells the result. Keep the comma before it.
compound-2.example: We can play outside, or we can bake cookies.

compound-3.title: Semicolons
compound-3.rule: A semicolon can join two complete sentences that belong together, with no joining word. Don't use a semicolon with and, but or so.
compound-3.example: The power went out; we played board games by flashlight.

complex-1.title: Joining with because, when, if
complex-1.rule: Join a complete sentence with a part that starts with because, when, if, after or before. That part tells why, when or what has to happen first.
complex-1.example: We stayed inside because it was raining.

complex-2.title: More joining words
complex-2.rule: Although and even though show a surprise. Until, while and since tell about time. When the joining part comes first, put a comma after it.
complex-2.example: Although it was cold, we played outside until dark.

complex-3.title: Commas in complex sentences
complex-3.rule: When a sentence starts with a part like Although, When or If, put a comma after that part. When that part comes at the end, leave the comma out.
complex-3.example: When the timer beeps, take the cookies out. Take the cookies out when the timer beeps.

flow-1.title: The Q&A Flow
flow-1.rule: Ask questions to find each word's job. Find the subject first: who or what? Then the verb: what is being said about it? Then adverbs (how? when? where?), adjectives (what kind? which one? how many?) and articles (a, an, the).
flow-1.example: The happy baby giggled. → A Adj SN V

flow-2.title: Prepositions and possessives
flow-2.rule: A preposition (P) like to, in or under starts a phrase, and its object (OP) answers what? or whom? after it. My, his and our are possessive pronoun adjectives (PPA); Sam's is a possessive noun adjective (PNA). A helping verb (HV) like is or were comes before the main verb.
flow-2.example: My dog is sleeping in the sun. → PPA SN HV V P A OP

flow-3.title: Objects and patterns
flow-3.rule: After the verb, ask what? or whom? A direct object (DO) makes the verb transitive (V-t). An indirect object (IO) tells to whom. After a linking verb (LV), a predicate noun (PrN) renames the subject, and a predicate adjective (PA) describes it.
flow-3.example: Sam kicked the ball. → SN V-t A DO, Pattern 2

case-1.title: I or me?
case-1.rule: Use I, he, she, we and they for the one doing the action, and me, him, her, us and them for the one getting it. Cover the other person to check: Sam and I went → I went. Myself only goes with I in the same sentence.
case-1.example: Mom drove Ava and me to practice. Sam and I built a robot.

case-2.title: Clear pronouns
case-2.rule: A pronoun has to point clearly to one noun. If it could mean two people or things, use the noun instead. Don't switch from they to you in the same sentence.
case-2.example: When Ana called Mia, Ana was upset. When students study, they remember more.

case-3.title: Who or whom?
case-3.rule: Use who where you could say he or she, and whom where you could say him or her. We and us work the same way before a noun: we students, us students.
case-3.example: Who called? (He called.) To whom did you write? (I wrote to him.)

proofread-1.title: Proofreading
proofread-1.rule: Read slowly, one sentence at a time. Check that verbs stay in the same tense, pronouns are right, and apostrophes and commas are where they belong. Each paragraph has 2 mistakes.
proofread-1.example: Last weekend we drive to the lake. → Last weekend we drove to the lake.

proofread-2.title: Proofreading: 3 mistakes
proofread-2.rule: Each paragraph has 3 mistakes. Check every verb against its subject and its time, and test every pronoun by covering the other person.
proofread-2.example: The players was proud. → The players were proud.

proofread-3.title: Proofreading: 4 mistakes
proofread-3.rule: Each paragraph has 4 mistakes, from any skill: tense, agreement, pronoun case, who and whom, apostrophes and sound-alike words.
proofread-3.example: To who should we write? → To whom should we write?

flow2-1.title: Questions and commands
flow2-1.rule: In a question, a helping or linking verb often comes first: Did the dog eat? Find the subject and verb the same way. A command has an understood subject, (You), labeled SP.
flow2-1.example: (You) Close the door. → SP V-t A DO, Pattern 2, imperative

flow2-2.title: Object complements
flow2-2.rule: After the direct object, ask: verb + DO + what? A noun that renames the DO is an object complement noun (OCN, Pattern 6). An adjective that describes it is an object complement adjective (OCA, Pattern 7).
flow2-2.example: The class named the hamster Peanut. (OCN, P6) The rain made the trail muddy. (OCA, P7)

flow2-3.title: All seven patterns
flow2-3.rule: Find the subject and verb, then look after the verb: nothing (P1), a DO (P2), an IO and DO (P3), a PrN (P4), a PA (P5), a DO and OCN (P6), or a DO and OCA (P7). Two subjects or two verbs joined by and, or or but are compound: label them CSN, CSP or CV, and the joining word C.
flow2-3.example: Grandma sent us a postcard. → SN V-t IO A DO, Pattern 3

aside-1.title: Hyphens and dashes
aside-1.rule: A hyphen (-) joins words that work together before a noun, like a well-known author, and numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine. A dash (—) is longer. It sets off a sudden break or an important add-on, with no spaces around it.
aside-1.example: My twenty-one-year-old cousin—a real chef—made dinner.

aside-2.title: Commas around extra information (parentheticals)
aside-2.rule: Extra information can come out without changing what the sentence means. Teachers and tests call it a parenthetical or nonrestrictive element. Put commas around it: a description added after a noun, a part starting with which, or an interrupter like however, of course, in fact or I think. Leave the commas out when the words tell which one you mean.
aside-2.example: My dog, a beagle, loves snow. The test, however, was easy. The dog that barks all night isn't mine.

aside-3.title: Dashes, parentheses and ellipses
aside-3.rule: A parenthetical can also go inside dashes or parentheses. Dashes make it stand out, and parentheses make it quieter; either way, one goes on each side. An ellipsis (…) shows a pause or that words were left out.
aside-3.example: The trip (all six hours of it) was worth it. Well… I think so.

types-1.title: Simple, compound, complex
types-1.rule: A simple sentence has one complete thought. A compound sentence joins two with a comma and and, but or so, or with a semicolon. A complex sentence has a complete thought plus a part that starts with a word like because, when or although.
types-1.example: I ran. I ran, and I won. Because I trained, I won.

types-2.title: Compound-complex sentences
types-2.rule: A compound-complex sentence has two complete thoughts plus at least one part that can't stand alone. Put a comma after a starting part, and a comma before and, but or so.
types-2.example: When the storm hit, the power went out, and we lit candles.

types-3.title: Sentence variety
types-3.rule: Mix short and long sentences. Combine choppy sentences with joining words so the meaning is clear, and keep the most important idea in the main part.
types-3.example: Choppy: It rained. We stayed in. We played chess. Better: Because it rained, we stayed in and played chess.

modifiers-1.title: Commas between adjectives
modifiers-1.rule: Put a comma between two adjectives when you could put and between them or switch their order: a long, cold night. Leave it out when you couldn't, as with numbers, sizes and colors: three big red apples.
modifiers-1.example: We walked through the dark, quiet woods to see a big gray owl.

modifiers-2.title: Misplaced and dangling modifiers
modifiers-2.rule: Put describing words right next to the word they describe. A describing phrase at the start of a sentence must be about the subject that comes right after it.
modifiers-2.example: Wrong: Covered in mud, Mom washed the dog. Right: Mom washed the dog, which was covered in mud.

modifiers-3.title: Active voice, passive voice and moods
modifiers-3.rule: In active voice, the subject does the action. In passive voice, the subject gets the action. Active is usually clearer. For a wish or something that isn't true, use were: I wish I were, if I were. Don't switch voice or mood partway through a sentence.
modifiers-3.example: Active: The class planted trees. Passive: Trees were planted by the class.

diagram-1.title: Diagram the subject and verb
diagram-1.rule: First mark up the sentence: circle the nouns, put a slash right before the verb, underline the complete subject once and the complete predicate twice. On the diagram, the subject and verb go on the long baseline, with a line between them that crosses it. Describing words go on slanted lines under the word they describe. A word like very or really that describes a describing word gets its own slanted line, joined to that word's line.
diagram-1.example: The small puppy ran quickly: puppy | ran on the baseline; The and small slant under puppy; quickly slants under ran.

diagram-2.title: Diagram phrases and complements
diagram-2.rule: A prepositional phrase hangs under the word it describes: the preposition on a slanted line, its object on a flat line. A direct object sits on the baseline after a short line that stops at the baseline. A predicate noun or adjective comes after a line that leans back toward the subject.
diagram-2.example: Sam kicked the ball: Sam | kicked | ball. The soup is hot: soup | is \ hot.

diagram-3.title: Indirect objects, object complements, questions and commands
diagram-3.rule: An indirect object hangs under the verb on a flat line, joined by an empty slanted line. An object complement follows the direct object after a line that leans back. Diagram a question as a statement, with the helping verb beside the verb. In a command, (You) is the subject. Compound subjects or verbs split the line into a fork: one part on each branch, with the conjunction beside a dashed line between them.
diagram-3.example: Mom gave Dad a gift: Mom | gave | gift, with Dad hanging under gave.

capitals-1.title: Capital letters: names, days and months
capitals-1.rule: Capitalize the first word of a sentence, the word I, names of people and pets, days of the week, months and holidays. The seasons (spring, summer, fall, winter) are not capitalized.
capitals-1.example: On Monday, Mia and I will plant tulips. They bloom in spring.

capitals-2.title: Capital letters: places, family names and titles
capitals-2.rule: Capitalize names of places, like Duluth, Lake Superior and Maple Street, and titles before a name, like Ms. Park, Dr. Lee and Aunt Rosa. Mom, Dad and Grandma get a capital when they're used as a name, but not after words like my or our.
capitals-2.example: My mom asked, "Dad, can Aunt Jen ride with us to Duluth?"

capitals-3.title: Capital letters: directions, regions, titles and languages
capitals-3.rule: North, south, east and west are lowercase when they tell a direction, but capitalized when they name a region, like the North Shore, the Midwest or North Dakota. Capitalize languages and nationalities, and the first, last and important words in titles. School subjects are lowercase, except languages like English and Spanish.
capitals-3.example: We drove north to the North Shore and read Charlotte's Web in English class.
